newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH FINANCE MINISTRY SILENT AMID ERM LEAK TALK.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH FINANCE MINISTRY SILENT AMID ERM LEAK TALK.

text.p: The finance ministry on Friday had no comment on Centre Party allegations in parliament late on Thursday that second finance minister Arja Alho had leaked information about the ERM peg during talks.
A ministry spokeswoman said neither finance minister Sauli Niinisto or Alho, or any of the ministry's senior officials, planned to make any official statement on Friday.

The Centre Party started exceptionally heated debate in the normally sanguine legislature with charges that Alho had leaked information about the link before the EU's monetary committee was over, media reported.

The chancellor of justice has been notified that there could have been "some sort of a problem" at the time of the link and will look into the issue, deputy chancellor of justice Jukka Pasanen told Reuters.
He declined to give any detail and said the chancellor would not be available for comment until Monday.
Finnish daily Aamulehti on Thursday said the accusations could potentially lead to an impeachment of Alho.

According to Centre Party MPs and member of the Bank of Finland's supervisory board Mauri Pekkarinen, Bank of Finland governor Sirkka Hamalainen told the supervisors on the night of October 12 when the markka was linked that Alho had signalled Finland's negotiation targets to Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn and commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy.
Pekkarinen and local media said this had happened while the monetary committe was still holding its decisive session.

Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen told parliament Alho had just acted according to instructions, contacting EU commissioner de Silguy, president Jacques Santer and Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn and giving them the range of Finland's targets.
"The central rate has not been given. That is not true," Paavo Lipponen said in parliament.

Pekkarinen made the charges against Alho after Lipponen had earned a reprimand from Speaker Riitta Uosukainen about his language and accusations to Centre party leader and former prime minister Esko Aho.
Some media reports said the incident had been staged, since Pekkarinen had diligently checked how to present the charges without offending parliamentary discipline.
However, in practice, Pekkarinen would probably not be liable anyway since parliamentary debate is virtually immune to legal action.
Charges could only be raised if a 5/6 majority of MPs voted in favour of them, a parliament spokesman told Reuters.
